en_revised: To the east of the pool created by Śakra (帝釋), in a forest, is the pool of the Dragon King Mucilinda (目支隣陀); its water is clear and dark, and its taste is sweet and delicious. On the west bank is a small shrine (精舍) containing an image of the Buddha. Formerly, when the Tathāgata had first attained supreme enlightenment, he sat here in meditation for seven days. At that time, this dragon king guarded the Tathāgata by coiling his body around the Buddha seven times and manifesting many heads that bowed down to form a canopy; therefore, his dwelling is located on the east bank of the pool.  To the east of the Mucilinda Dragon Pool, in a forest shrine, there is an image of the Buddha in an emaciated state. Beside it is a place for walking meditation, more than seventy paces long, with a pippala (卑鉢羅) tree at both the north and south ends. Therefore, among the local people today, those who are afflicted with illness often apply scented oil to the image and frequently receive relief and recovery.  This is the place where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities. In order to subdue the non-Buddhists and also because he accepted the request of Māra, the Tathāgata practiced austerities for six years, eating one hemp seed and one grain of wheat per day. His appearance became haggard and his body became emaciated; when walking back and forth, he would grasp the trees to rise. Beside the pippala tree where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities, there is a stūpa; this is the place where Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如) and the other four men resided. Initially, when the prince renounced his home, wandering through mountains and marshes and resting in forests and by springs, King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) ordered these five men to follow and attend to him. Once the prince practiced austerities, Kauṇḍinya and the others also diligently sought the way.

issues: "the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata witnessed various divine transformations and had karmic connections" → 見諸神變化有緣處 (見 = 現) "where the Tathāgata displayed miracles to convert those with whom he had affinity" (the next stūpa is "beside the place where he displayed the miracles", 現神變側); "the three brothers, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his followers, as well as their one thousand disciples" → 優樓頻螺迦葉波三兄弟及千門人 "the three Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa brothers and their thousand disciples"; "The two hundred disciples of Gayā-Kāśyapa, hearing that their elder brother…" → Gayā-Kāśyapa with his two hundred disciples, hearing that his elder brother(s) had given up their practice, also came; "the Kāśyapa brothers promoted their supernatural powers" → 時推神通 "were esteemed in their day for their supernatural powers"
en_revised: Southeast of the place where Kauṇḍinya and his companions resided, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva entered the Nairañjanā River to bathe. Not far from the riverbank is the place where the Bodhisattva received the milk-rice. Beside that is a stūpa marking the place where the two elders offered parched grain and honey. The Buddha sat under a tree in the cross-legged position, silent and still, experiencing the joy of liberation; after seven days had passed, he finally arose from meditation. At that time, two merchant leaders were passing by the edge of the forest, and the deity of that forest told the merchant leaders, "The Prince of the Śākya clan is now within this wood; he has just attained the fruit of Buddhahood and his mind is concentrated in silent meditation. He has not eaten for forty-nine days; if you offer him whatever you have, you will obtain great and wholesome benefit." The two merchant leaders then each took their travel provisions of parched grain and honey to offer to him, and the World-Honored One accepted them. Beside the place where the elders offered the parched grain, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Four Heavenly Kings offered alms bowls. After the merchant leaders had offered the parched grain and honey, the World-Honored One considered what vessel he should use to receive them. At that time, the four heavenly kings came from the four directions, each holding a golden bowl to offer to him. The World-Honored One remained silent and did not accept them, thinking that such vessels were not appropriate for one who has left the household life. The four heavenly kings set aside the golden bowls and offered silver ones, and even bowls of crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, musaragalva, and pearl, but the World-Honored One would not accept any of them. The four heavenly kings each returned to their palaces and brought back stone bowls, dark blue and translucent, which they presented again. To avoid favoring one over the others, the World-Honored One accepted them all, stacked them in sequence, and pressed them into a single bowl; therefore, on the outside, there are four ridges. Not far from the place where the four heavenly kings offered the bowls, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for his mother. After the Tathāgata had attained perfect enlightenment and was acclaimed as the teacher of gods and men, his mother, Māyā, descended from the heavenly palace to this place, and the World-Honored One, according to her capacity, manifested teachings to bring her benefit and joy. Beside it, on the bank of a dried-up pond, there is a stūpa; this is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata displayed miracles to convert those with whom he had affinity. Beside the place where he manifested divine transformations, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata converted the three brothers Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (優樓頻螺迦葉波) and the others, together with their one thousand disciples. As the Tathāgata was setting forth the good path and subduing them according to their dispositions, the five hundred disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa requested to receive the Buddha’s teaching. Kāśyapa said, "I shall also return from the path of delusion along with you." Thereupon, they followed one another and came to the place of the Buddha. The Tathāgata told them, "Discard your deer-skin garments and abandon your fire-worship implements." At that time, the Brahmins respectfully accepted the holy teaching and cast their robes and implements into the Nairañjanā River. Nadī-Kāśyapa (捺地迦葉波) saw the sacrificial vessels floating down the current and, together with his disciples, waited to see what his elder brother would do; having seen him change his course, he also followed suit and dyed his robes. Gayā-Kāśyapa (伽耶迦葉波) with his two hundred disciples, hearing that his elder brother had abandoned his former practice, also came to the place of the Buddha and wished to practice the holy life. To the northwest of the place where the Kāśyapa brothers were converted is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata subdued the fire dragon that the Kāśyapas worshipped. When the Tathāgata was about to convert those people and overcome what they revered, he stayed in the chamber of the Brahmins' fire dragon. After midnight, the dragon exhaled smoke and flames. The Buddha, having entered into samādhi, also emitted a fiery light, so that the chamber was brightly illuminated with fierce and blazing flames. The Brahmin masters, fearing the fire would harm the Buddha, all rushed toward it, crying out in sorrow and pity. Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (優樓頻螺迦葉波) said to his disciples, "Looking at it now, this may not be a fire; it must be that the Śramaṇa has subdued the fire dragon." The Tathāgata then placed the fire dragon into his alms bowl and, at dawn, held it up to show the disciples of the non-Buddhists. The stūpa beside this is the place where five hundred pratyekabuddhas (獨覺) entered nirvāṇa together. The stūpa to the south of the Mucilinda (目支隣陀) Dragon Pool is the place where Kāśyapa rescued the Tathāgata from drowning. At that time, the Kāśyapa brothers were esteemed for their supernatural powers, and people from far and near admired their virtue, with the masses turning their hearts toward them. The World-honored One, intending to guide the deluded disciples, employed great skillful means to transform them; he raised dense clouds and caused a violent rain to fall, which surrounded the place where the Buddha resided, leaving it alone without water. Seeing this cloud and rain, Kāśyapa said to his disciples, "Will the Śramaṇa’s dwelling not be flooded?" He set out in a boat to rescue him, only to see the World-honored One walking on the water as if it were dry land; as he stepped into the middle of the river, the waters parted and the sand appeared. Having seen this, Kāśyapa’s heart was subdued and he withdrew.

en_revised: East of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, crossing the Nairañjanā River, there is a stūpa in a great forest. To its north is a pond, which is the place where a fragrant elephant (gandhahastin) attended to his mother. In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he was a young fragrant elephant living in the northern mountains, who would roam by the side of this pond. His mother was blind, and he would gather lotus roots and draw clear water, respectfully performing his filial duties and adapting to the changing seasons. It happened that a man, wandering in the forest and losing his way, paced back and forth, wailing and crying in distress. The young elephant heard him and, feeling compassion, guided him to show him the way home. Once the man had returned, he reported to the king, saying, "I know of a fragrant elephant wandering in the forest thickets; this is a rare treasure, and you may go to capture it." The king accepted his words and raised an army to go hunting. The man acted as a guide, but the moment he pointed out the elephant to the king, both his arms fell off as if they had been severed. Although the king was startled by this strange event, he still bound the young elephant and brought him back. After the young elephant had been tied up for a long time, he would not eat grass or drink water. The stable keeper reported this to the king, who then went in person to question him. The young elephant said, "My mother is blind and has been starving for days; now that I am suffering in captivity, how could I find food sweet?" The king, feeling compassion for his situation, released him. Beside this is a stūpa, with a stone pillar erected in front, which is the place where the Buddha Kāśyapa (迦葉波佛) once sat in meditation. Nearby are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

issues: "The people of the country have long wished to see this, and have heard of it for a long time." → 國人願覩，聞之久矣 "I have long heard that the people of the country wish to see it"; the speech is also split by a stray quote mark; "the body of a leopard" → 狸身 "the body of a wildcat"
en_revised: To the east of where the four Buddhas sat, one crosses the Mahā (莫訶河) River and arrives in a great forest, where there is a stone pillar; this is the place where a non-Buddhist practitioner entered into meditation and made an evil vow. In the past, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子), whose aspirations transcended the mists and clouds, and whose body abandoned the marshes and thickets; he dwelt in this forest of the Dharma, hiding his spirit and concealing his traces. Having attained the five supernatural powers, he achieved the meditation of the peak of existence (bhavāgra). The King of Magadha (摩揭陀王) held him in particularly deep respect and, every day at noon, invited him to the palace for a meal. Udraka Rāmaputra would soar through the void and walk upon the air, coming and going without fail. The King of Magadha would watch and wait for the appointed time; once he arrived, the king would personally receive him and escort him to his seat.  When the king was about to depart on a tour and wished to entrust his affairs to someone, he examined those in the inner palace, but found no one capable of undertaking the command. He had a young daughter of virtuous and prudent character; she was both close to him and wise, with none surpassing her, so the King of Magadha summoned her and commanded: "I am about to travel far and have something to entrust to you; you should be diligent and see this matter through to the end with care. That immortal Udraka Rāmaputra is one whom I have long held in respect; when the time comes for him to arrive for his meal, treat him just as I have done."  Having given these instructions, the king departed on his tour. The young lady accepted the command and waited upon him according to the rites; when the great immortal arrived, she supported him and assisted him to his seat. Once Udraka Rāmaputra had touched the woman, desire for the realm of sense-objects arose, and he regressed, losing his supernatural powers. When he had finished his meal and spoke of returning, he was unable to soar through the void. Feeling ashamed and humiliated in his heart, he deceitfully said to the woman: "I have recently been cultivating the path, entering into meditation to soothe my spirit, and have been soaring through the void to come and go, having almost no leisure time. I have long heard that the people of the country wish to see this. However, the sages of old have left us instructions that benefiting others is our primary duty; how could I remain content with my own virtue and forget the need to assist others? I now wish to depart through the gate and travel by treading upon the ground, so that all those who see me may receive blessings and benefit." Having heard this, the king’s daughter made the announcement far and near. At that time, people rushed to compete, sweeping and cleaning the roads, and hundreds of thousands of people stood waiting to see his arrival. Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) walked from the royal palace to that religious forest and sat in meditation, but his mind wandered to external environments; when he stayed in the forest, the birds chirped, and when he approached the pond, the fish and turtles made noise, so that his feelings were distracted and his mind disturbed, causing him to lose his concentration and abandon his meditation. He then gave rise to anger and immediately made an evil vow: "May I in the future become a fierce and wicked beast with the body of a wildcat and the wings of a bird to seize and eat living creatures; let my body be three thousand li wide, with two wings each fifteen hundred li wide, so that I may enter the forests to devour the feathered tribes and enter the currents to eat the aquatic beings." Having made this vow, his anger gradually subsided, and after practicing diligently for a while, he regained his original concentration. Not long after, he passed away and was born in the Heaven of the First Existence (第一有天), with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas. The Tathāgata predicted that once his heavenly lifespan was exhausted, he would fulfill his former vow and obtain this wretched body. From that point on, he would wander through the evil paths, with no time set for his liberation.

issues: "Six out of every ten students who received his teachings were his disciples" (circular) → 受業門人，十室而六 "disciples receiving instruction came from six households out of ten" (Mizutani reads 室 as rooms: his disciples filled six rooms out of ten)
en_revised: Traveling more than thirty *li* eastward through the empty valleys of the mountain of Buddhavana (佛陀伐那山), one reaches the forest of Yaṣṭi (洩瑟知林). The bamboo in this forest is tall and slender, covering the mountains and filling the valleys. Long ago, there was a Brahmin who, having heard that the body of the Buddha Śākyamuni was sixteen feet tall, constantly harbored doubts and could not believe it; he therefore took a sixteen-foot bamboo staff, intending to measure the Buddha’s body. Constantly, the staff would extend beyond sixteen feet at its tip; as it thus increased in height, he was unable to reach the truth of it, so he threw the staff away and departed, whereupon it took root. Within the forest is a large stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here manifesting great supernatural powers for the sake of gods and men, and expounding the profound and subtle Dharma.  Recently, in the Staff Forest, there was an upāsaka named Jayasena (闍耶犀那), who belonged to the Kṣatriya caste of Western India. His aspirations were for simplicity and ease, his heart delighted in the mountains and forests, and while his physical traces resided in this illusory realm, his mind roamed the boundaries of ultimate truth. He thoroughly investigated the subtle mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, his eloquence was noble and lofty, and his demeanor was refined and elegant. Śramaṇas, Brahmins, followers of non-Buddhist paths, heterodox scholars, kings, ministers, elders, and the wealthy and influential all flocked to visit him, bowing their heads to request instruction. Disciples receiving instruction from him came from six households out of ten. He was approaching seventy years of age, yet he studied with tireless devotion; he abandoned all other arts and practiced only the Buddhist scriptures, exerting his body and mind without ceasing day or night. According to the custom of India, scented powder is mixed into clay to make miniature stūpas five or six inches high, into which written scriptures are placed; these are called Dharma relics. As their numbers gradually accumulate, a large stūpa is built to house them all together, where offerings are constantly performed. Thus, the practice of Jayasena (勝軍) was such that his mouth would proclaim the wonderful Dharma to guide and encourage students, while his hands would make stūpas to cultivate superior merit. At night, he would practice walking meditation, chanting, and sitting in quiet contemplation, never finding time for sleep or food, exerting himself day and night without slackening. He reached one hundred years of age, yet his resolve and work did not decline. Over a period of thirty years, he made a total of seven koṭis of Dharma-relic stūpas. Each time he completed one koṭi, he built a large stūpa to house them all, where he grandly performed offerings and invited the monastic assembly to celebrate with a religious ceremony. At those times, a divine light would shine brilliantly as a manifest miracle, and from then on, it would emit light from time to time.

issues: "a great mountain (Pravaragiri)" → 大山 only; Pravaragiri is the different "great mountain" of 08.04.02 (Barābar), not this one near Rājagṛha
en_revised: More than ten *li* to the southwest of the Stick Wood (Yaṣṭivana), on the southern slope of a great mountain, there are two hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the past, the Tathāgata manifested this water and bathed therein. They still exist today with their clear flow undiminished; people from near and far all come to bathe in them, and there are none among those with chronic illnesses or old ailments who are not cured. Beside them is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata once walked.

issues: "the great mountain (Pravaragiri)" → 大山 only; the Pravaragiri gloss belongs to 08.04.02 (Mizutani identifies this one as Handia hill)
en_revised: Traveling six or seven li southeast from the Yaṣṭi Wood (杖林), one reaches a great mountain. In front of a transverse ridge stands a stone stupa where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma to humans and devas for two or three months. At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王), wishing to come and hear the Dharma, cleared the mountain and piled up stones to build a staircase for his ascent, measuring over twenty paces in width and three or four li in length.

issues: "the great mountain (Pravaragiri)" → 大山 only (cf. 09.02.03a); "an isolated hill (Vyāsa)" → the hill is not named Vyāsa; only the ṛṣi is
en_revised: Three or four li to the north of the great mountain is an isolated hill (孤山), where in the past the Rishi Vyāsa (廣博仙人) lived in seclusion. He chiseled into the cliff to create a chamber, the remains of which still exist. He transmitted his teachings to his disciples, and his legacy still prevails.

issues: "the Isolated Hill (Vyāsa)" / "the Small Isolated Hill (Asura)" → 孤山, 小孤山 carry no such names (the asura palace is the cavern); "there were some curious individuals deeply skilled in magical arts who gathered their companions" → 往有好事者，深閑呪術，顧儔命侶，十有四人 "a curious man versed in spells gathered companions, fourteen in all" (one magician; hence 唯彼術士 and 餘十三人)
en_revised: Four or five li to the northeast of the Isolated Hill (孤山) is a Small Isolated Hill (小孤山). In the cliffside of the mountain is a stone chamber, vast and spacious, capable of seating over a thousand people; in the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for three months. Above the stone chamber is a large flat rock where Śakra and the Brahmā King ground ox-head sandalwood to anoint the Buddha’s body; the lingering fragrance on the rock remains potent to this day. In the southwest corner of the stone chamber is a rocky cavern, which the people of India call the Palace of the Asuras (阿素洛宮).  In the past, there was a curious man deeply skilled in magical arts who gathered companions, fourteen people in all, and having made a pact to share the same intent, they entered this rocky cavern. After traveling thirty or forty li, it suddenly became brightly illuminated, and they saw cities, towers, and pavilions, all made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli. Once these people arrived, there were various young maidens standing by the gates who joyfully welcomed them and treated them with great courtesy. They then gradually advanced to the inner city gate, where two maidservants, each holding a golden tray filled with flowers and incense, came to greet them. They said to the group, "It is fitting that you go to the pool to bathe, and anoint yourselves and adorn your heads with fragrant flowers; only after doing so should you enter, for this would be beautiful. Only that master of arts should proceed quickly."  The other thirteen people then immediately bathed. Once they had entered the pool, they felt as if they had forgotten everything, and they found themselves sitting in a rice paddy in a flat plain to the north of this place, already thirty or forty li away. Beside the stone chamber is a plank path, more than ten paces wide and four or five li long. In the past, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was about to go to the place of the Buddha, he cut through rocks to open the valley and leveled cliffs to fill the ravines; he either piled up stones or excavated the cliffs to create steps, so as to reach the place of the Buddha.

issues: "this great mountain (Pravaragiri)" → 大山 only; "realized the three-fold bodhi" → 證三菩提 "realized saṃbodhi (perfect enlightenment)" (三菩提 transcribes saṃbodhi); "translated into Chinese as 'Shengmi' (勝密)" → the text gives no such note; it simply switches to the Chinese name 勝密
en_revised: From this great mountain, traveling east for more than sixty *li*, one arrives at the city of Kuśāgrapura (矩奢掲羅補羅城). This is the "City of the Superior Thatch" (Kuśāgrapura), located in the center of the kingdom of Magadha and the capital of ancient kings; it is called the "City of Superior Thatch" because it produces an abundance of excellent and auspicious fragrant reeds. Lofty mountains surround it, serving as an outer wall; to the west, it connects to a mountain pass, and to the north, it opens to a mountain gate. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, with a circumference of more than one hundred and fifty *li*. The remaining foundations of the inner city have a circumference of more than thirty *li*. *Karṇikāra* trees (羯尼迦樹) cover all the paths; their flowers contain a unique fragrance, and their color is as brilliant as gold. In the month of late spring, the forests are all golden.  Outside the north gate of the palace city is a *stūpa*, marking the place where Devadatta, having become an intimate friend of King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王), released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla (護財) in an attempt to harm the Tathāgata. From the tips of the Tathāgata’s fingers, five lions emerged, and the intoxicated elephant was subdued here and moved forward. To the northeast of the place where the intoxicated elephant was subdued is a *stūpa*, marking the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) attained the fruit of sainthood upon hearing the Dharma preached by the *bhikṣu* Aśvajit (阿濕婆恃).   Previously, when Śāriputra was a householder, he possessed high talent and refined character, and was highly regarded at that time; his students and disciples received instruction from him. At this time, he was about to enter the great city of Rājagṛha (王舍大城), and the *bhikṣu* Aśvajit was also just then begging for food. At that time, Śāriputra saw Aśvajit from afar and said to his students, "That person coming here is very composed and dignified. If he had not attained the holy fruit, how could he be so disciplined and tranquil? We should wait a little while to observe his demeanor." The bhikṣu Aśvajit (馬勝) had already attained the state of an arhat; his mind had attained freedom, his demeanor was harmonious and refined, and he approached with the rhythmic shaking of his khakkhara staff. Śāriputra said, "Elder, are you well and at peace? Who is your teacher, and what dharma have you realized that makes you so joyful and composed?" Aśvajit replied to him, "Do you not know? The crown prince of King Śuddhodana (淨飯王), who renounced the position of a wheel-turning monarch, felt compassion for the six destinies, practiced austerities for six years, realized *saṃbodhi* (三菩提), and possesses all-encompassing wisdom—he is my teacher. As for the dharma, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is difficult to explain or categorize. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully describe it; how could one as foolish and ignorant as I be able to discuss it in detail?" He then recited a verse in praise of the Buddha-dharma. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra attained the fruit.  Not far to the north of where Śāriputra attained the fruit, there is a large, deep pit with a stūpa built beside it; this is the place where Śrīgupta (室利毱多; Chin. 勝密, "Shengmi") attempted to harm the Buddha with a fire pit and poisoned food. This Shengmi was a follower of the non-Buddhist paths and was deeply attached to erroneous views. The various Brahmins had said to him, "Gautama is respected by the people of the country, which has left our followers with nothing to rely on. You should now invite him to your home for a feast; dig a large pit at the gate, fill it with fire, bridge it with rotten wood, and cover it with dry earth. All the food and drink should be mixed with poison; if he escapes the fire pit, he will surely encounter the poisoned food." Shengmi accepted their command and prepared the poisoned feast. The people of the city, all knowing that Shengmi had harbored evil and harmful intentions toward the World-Honored One, collectively urged and requested the Buddha not to go. The World-Honored One replied, "Do not harbor worry. The body of the Tathāgata cannot be harmed by anything." Thereupon, he accepted the invitation and went. As his foot stepped upon the threshold, the fire pit turned into a pool, its clear waters reflecting like a mirror and filled with blooming lotuses. Having seen this, Shengmi (Śrīgupta) was filled with panic and confusion, and said to his disciples, "Even if he has escaped the fire by means of magic, there is still the poisoned food." When the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he expounded the wonderful Dharma for them; having heard this, Shengmi confessed his faults and took refuge.

issues: "During the fifty years" → 垂五十年 "nearly fifty years"
en_revised: Traveling fourteen or fifteen li northeast from the palace city, one reaches the mountain of Gṛdhrakūṭa (姞栗陀羅矩吒山). It adjoins the southern slope of the North Mountain and rises solitary and steep; it serves as a dwelling for vultures and resembles a lofty terrace, where the empty sky and the verdant peaks reflect one another, their colors varying in depth and lightness. During the nearly fifty years that the Tathāgata presided over the world, he resided much on this mountain, extensively expounding the subtle Dharma. For the sake of hearing the Dharma, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) mobilized laborers to build a path from the foot of the mountain to the summit, spanning valleys and scaling rocks, laying stones to form steps more than ten paces wide and five or six li in length. Midway along the path are two small stūpas: one is called "Dismounting" (下乘), marking the spot where the king would proceed on foot; the other is called "Turning Back the Ordinary" (退凡), marking where he would screen out ordinary people, not allowing them to proceed further. The summit of the mountain is long from east to west and narrow from north to south.

issues: "vihara (mūla-gandha-kuṭī 根本香殿)" → the text has only 精舍; the gloss is not in the text; "the city of Magadha (摩揭陀國)" → text 摩揭陀城
en_revised: On the western edge of the cliff stands a brick vihara (精舍), of lofty and spacious, extraordinary construction, with its door opening to the east. In the past, the Tathāgata often resided here to expound the Dharma; today, there is an image of him expounding the Dharma, equal in measure to the body of the Tathāgata. To the east of the vihara is a long stone, which is where the Tathāgata walked during his meditative perambulations. Beside it is a large stone, fourteen or fifteen feet high and over thirty paces in circumference; this is the place where Devadatta threw a rock from afar to strike the Buddha. Below the cliff to the south is a stūpa where, in the past, the Tathāgata expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (法花經). On the side of the mountain cliff to the south of the vihara is a large stone chamber where the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration in the past. To the northwest of the Buddha’s stone chamber, in front of a cave, is a large flat rock; this is the place where Ānanda was terrified by Māra. While the Venerable Ānanda was in meditative concentration here, the Demon King transformed himself into a vulture; during the dark phase of the moon, it perched upon the large rock, flapping its wings and shrieking to frighten the Venerable One. At that time, the Venerable One was terrified and at a loss. The Tathāgata, perceiving this, reached out his hand to comfort him, passing through the stone wall to stroke Ānanda’s head, and addressed him with words of great compassion: "This is a transformation by Māra; you should have no fear." Having received this comfort, Ānanda’s body and mind became peaceful and joyful. The bird’s tracks on the stone and the hole through the cliff, though much time has passed, still remain today. Beside the vihara are several stone chambers where Śāriputra and other great Arhats entered into meditative concentration. In front of Śāriputra’s stone chamber is a large well; though it is dried up and waterless, its ruins and hollow still remain. In the stony gully to the northeast of the vihara is a large flat rock, which is the place where the Tathāgata dried his kaṣāya; the patterns of the robe are clear and distinct, as bright as if they were carved. Beside it, on the rock, are the footprints of the Buddha; although the wheel markings are faint, their shape and form can still be discerned. On the summit of the north mountain is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata gazed toward the city of Magadha (摩揭陀城) and preached the Dharma for seven days.

en_revised: To the west of the hot springs is the Pippala (卑鉢羅) stone cave, where the World-Honored One used to dwell constantly in the past. The cavern in the rear wall is the palace of the Asuras (阿素洛). Many bhikṣus who practice meditation reside in this chamber. At times, strange and monstrous forms of dragons, snakes, and lions appear; those who see them become mentally deranged. However, because this is a superior site where the holy and sagely have dwelt, those who follow in their footsteps and admire their influence forget the disasters and calamities associated with it. Recently, there was a bhikṣu of pure conduct who delighted in quiet seclusion and wished to hide away in this chamber to practice meditation. Someone cautioned him, saying, "Do not go there. It is full of disasters and strange occurrences, causing no small amount of harm. It is difficult to attain concentration there, and I fear you will lose your life. You should take warning from past events and not leave cause for later regret." The bhikṣu replied, "That is not so. I am determined to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and to subdue the heavenly demons; if this is the harm you speak of, how is it worth mentioning?" He then shook his khakkhara-staff and went to the chamber. There, he set up an altar and recited protective mantras. After ten days, a young woman emerged from the cavern and said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable one, you wear the dyed robes and keep the precepts, serving as a refuge for sentient beings; you cultivate wisdom and practice meditation, acting as a virtuous guide for living creatures. Yet now you dwell here and terrify us. Is this the teaching of the Tathāgata?" The bhikṣu replied, "I observe the pure precepts and follow the holy teachings. I hide my tracks in the mountain valleys to stay far from noise and confusion. Why do you suddenly reproach me for this?" She replied, "When you recite your mantras, the sound goes forth, and fire enters from outside, burning my dwelling and afflicting my kin. I only pray that you have compassion and do not recite the mantras again." The bhikṣu said, "I recite the mantras for self-protection, not because I wish to harm living beings. In the past, when practitioners dwelt here to practice meditation, hoping to attain the holy fruit to save those in the dark paths, they saw your monstrosity and were terrified, losing their lives; this was your fault, so what excuse do you have?" She replied, "My karmic obstructions are heavy and my wisdom is shallow. From now on, I shall live in seclusion and keep to my place; I also hope that you, Venerable Sir, will not recite the divine mantras." The bhikṣu then practiced meditation as before, in peace and without harm. On Mount Vipula (毘布羅山) there is a stūpa, the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma in the past. Nowadays, many naked heretics (nirgrantha) reside here, practicing austerities without negligence day or night; from dawn until dusk, they turn around and observe the sun.

issues: "the Great Stone Chamber (Dakṣiṇagiri)" → 大石室 only; Dakṣiṇagiri (南山) belongs to the First-Council cave, 09.02.16
en_revised: To the left of the north gate of the mountain city, on the shaded side of the southern cliff, traveling east for two or three li, one arrives at a great stone chamber; in the past, Devadatta entered into meditation here. Not far to the east of the stone chamber, there are colored streaks on a flat rock that appear as if stained with blood, and beside it stands a stūpa built at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation took his own life and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who exerted his mind and body, living in seclusion to practice meditation; as the years passed, he did not attain the holy fruit. Retiring and blaming himself, he sighed privately, saying: "The fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa) is not attained in time; what is the use of living in this body burdened with defilements!" He then went to this rock and stabbed his own neck; at that moment, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, rose into the void, manifested spiritual transformations, transformed into fire to consume his body, and entered into extinction (parinirvāṇa). Admiring his noble conduct, they built this to record his merit. On the cliff to the east of where the bhikṣu attained the fruit, there is a stone stūpa at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation threw himself from the cliff and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who sat in the mountain forests practicing the meditation for attaining the fruit; though he had been diligent for a long time, he could not realize the fruit, yet he continued his contemplation day and night without forgetting his tranquil meditation. The Tathāgata, knowing that his faculties were about to ripen, went there to bring it to completion; he traveled from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana) to the foot of the mountain cliff, snapped his fingers to summon him, and stood waiting. Seeing the Holy One from afar, the bhikṣu felt great joy in body and mind and threw himself from the cliff; because of his pure heart and his respectful faith in the Buddha's words, he attained the fruit of sainthood before reaching the ground. The World-Honored One said, "You should know that now is the time." He then ascended into the void and manifested miraculous transformations. This was to make manifest his pure faith, and therefore this memorial was established.

issues: "monastery (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī)" → 精舍 = vihāra; the technical term is not in the text
en_revised: Traveling more than one *li* from the north gate of the mountain city, one arrives at the Kalandaka Bamboo Garden (迦蘭陀竹園; Skt. Veṇuvana-kalandakanivāpa). There is now a vihāra (精舍) here with a stone foundation and brick chambers, with its entrance opening to the east. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he often resided here, expounding the Dharma and transforming beings, guiding the ordinary and rescuing the worldly. Now, an image of the Tathāgata’s body has been made.  Formerly, there was a great elder in this city named Kalandaka, who was renowned for his wealth and nobility at that time. He had donated a large bamboo grove to the non-Buddhists. When he saw the Tathāgata and heard the Dharma, he developed pure faith. He reflected on how he had previously allowed the bamboo grove to be occupied by those of other sects, while the Teacher of Gods and Men now had no place to lodge. At that time, various spirits and deities, moved by his sincerity, expelled the non-Buddhists and told them, "The elder Kalandaka intends to build a Buddhist monastery in the bamboo grove; you should depart quickly to avoid danger and calamity." The non-Buddhists were resentful and departed in anger. The elder then established the monastery here; once the work was completed, he went in person to invite the Buddha, and the Tathāgata thereupon accepted his offering.

issues: "As for the others who are still in the stage of learning" → 自餘果學 "the rest, whether holders of a fruit or learners"
en_revised: Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), on the northern side of the South Mountain (Dakṣiṇagiri), in a great bamboo forest, there is a large stone chamber. This is where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with nine hundred and ninety great arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Tathāgata’s nirvana. In front are the old foundations of a hall built by King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) for the great arhats who were to compile the Dharma-treasury.  Initially, while Mahākāśyapa was sitting in meditation in the mountain forest, he suddenly saw a brilliant light and observed the earth quake. He said, “What omen is this, that it should be so extraordinary?” Using his heavenly eye to observe, he saw that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvana between the twin trees, and he immediately ordered his followers to hasten to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). On the road, he met a Brahman holding a heavenly flower in his hand. Mahākāśyapa asked, “Where do you come from? Do you know where my Great Teacher is now?” The Brahman replied, “I have just come from that city of Kuśinagara; I saw that your Great Teacher has already entered nirvana, and the multitudes of gods and men are all making offerings. The flower I hold was obtained from there.”  Upon hearing this, Mahākāśyapa said to his followers, “The sun of wisdom has set, the world is in darkness, the excellent guide has departed, and sentient beings will fall into ruin.” Lax monks congratulated one another, saying, “The Tathāgata has attained extinction, so we are now at ease. If we commit any offense, who will be able to rebuke or restrain us?” Hearing this, Mahākāśyapa was deeply grieved and thought to compile the Dharma-treasury to govern offenses according to the teachings. He then went to the twin trees to view the transformation and pay his respects. Soon after, the Dharma King passed away; humans and gods were left without a guide, and the great arhats also entered parinirvāṇa. At that time, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself, "In obedience to the Buddha’s teachings, it is fitting to compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, he ascended Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山), struck the great ghaṇṭa (大揵稚), and proclaimed: "A Dharma assembly is about to be held in the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城); all those who have realized the fruits of the path should assemble here with all speed!" The sound of the ghaṇṭa carried the teaching of Kāśyapa, reaching throughout the trichiliomegachiliocosm (三千大千世界), and all who possessed supernatural powers heard it and gathered.  At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered extinction, and the world is empty. We must compile the Dharma-treasury to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Now, in compiling the Dharma, we must prioritize simplicity and quietude; how can we rely on a large crowd and fail to accomplish this noble task? Those who possess the three knowledges (三明), have attained the six supernatural powers (六通), whose retention of what they have heard is unerring, and whose eloquence is unimpeded—such superior persons may participate in the compilation. As for the rest, whether holders of a fruit or learners, each should return to their own dwelling."  Thus, nine hundred and ninety people were obtained. Excluding Ānanda, who was still in the stage of learning, Mahākāśyapa summoned him and said, "You have not yet exhausted the outflows; you should leave the assembly of sages." Ānanda replied, "I have attended upon the Tathāgata for many years, and whenever there were discussions on the Dharma, I was never excluded. Now that the compilation is to take place, I am being expelled; the Dharma King has entered extinction, and I have lost my refuge." Kāśyapa told him, "Do not harbor sorrow or distress. You have personally attended upon the Buddha and are indeed very learned, but your attachments and delusions are not yet exhausted, and your habitual bonds are not yet severed." Ānanda, his arguments exhausted, withdrew to a quiet and secluded place. He wished to attain the state of the non-learner (aśaikṣa), but despite his diligent efforts, he could not realize it. Having become weary and exhausted, he intended to take a short rest; before his head had even touched the pillow, he attained the state of an Arhat. He went to the place of the assembly and knocked on the door to announce his arrival. Kāśyapa asked, "Have you exhausted your defilements? You should employ your supernatural powers and enter without using the door." Ānanda accepted the command, entered through the keyhole, paid homage to the monks, and withdrew to sit in his place. This was on the fifteenth day of the first month of the summer retreat.  Thereupon, Kāśyapa proclaimed aloud, "Reflect and listen carefully! Ānanda, who has heard and retained the teachings, and whom the Tathāgata praised, shall compile the Sūtra-piṭaka (素呾纜藏). Upāli, who has mastered the Vinaya and is recognized by the assembly, shall compile the Vinaya-piṭaka (毘奈耶藏). I, Kāśyapa, shall compile the Abhidharma-piṭaka (阿毘達磨藏)." After two or three months had passed, the compilation of the three piṭakas was completed. Because Mahākāśyapa was the senior elder (sthavira) among the monks, the group was consequently called the Sthavira school (上座部).  To the northwest of where Mahākāśyapa held the assembly, there is a stūpa (窣堵波). This is the place where Ānanda, having been rebuked by the monks and excluded from the assembly, came to sit in meditation and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Only after attaining this fruit was he permitted to participate.

issues: "the elder Jotipāla (珠底色迦)" → 珠底色迦 transcribes Jyotiṣka (the householder Jyotiṣka of the Vinaya legends); Jotipāla is a different name
en_revised: Not far to the northeast of the stone pillar, one arrives at the city of Rājagṛhī (曷羅闍姞利呬城). The outer wall has already collapsed, and no remains of the ramparts are left; although the inner city is ruined, its foundations are still steep and high, measuring more than twenty *li* in circumference, with one gate on each side. Formerly, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) had his capital in the Upper Palace City, the households of the registered inhabitants frequently suffered from the calamity of fire. If one family was negligent, the neighbors on all four sides would suffer the disaster; the people had no time for anything but fire prevention, their properties and livelihoods were abandoned, and the masses lived in grievance and unrest. The king said, "Because of my lack of virtue, the common people suffer; what merit can I cultivate to avert this?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous transformation is harmonious and peaceful, and your governance and teachings are clear and discerning. Now, these common people are not cautious, leading to these fire disasters. It is fitting to establish a strict code to prevent future offenses. If a fire breaks out, investigate thoroughly to find who started it first, punish the chief culprit, and banish them to the Cold Forest (寒林)." The Cold Forest is a place where corpses are abandoned; it is commonly called an inauspicious place, and people have ceased all tracks of travel there. "Now, to banish them there is the same as abandoning them like a corpse. Being ashamed of such a lowly dwelling, they will naturally be cautious and protective." The king said, "Good; it should be announced everywhere to the residents." Shortly after, a fire broke out in the king’s own palace first. He said to his ministers, "I shall move." He then ordered the crown prince to supervise the affairs of the capital, and wishing to clarify the laws of the state, he moved his residence there. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐王), hearing that King Bimbisāra was living in the open at the Cold Forest, assembled his troops with the intent to launch a surprise attack. The border scouts reported this, and he then built the city. Because the king first resided here, it is called the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). The officials, the gentry, and the common people all moved their households there. Some say that it was not until King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) that this city was built; once the crown prince Ajātaśatru succeeded to the throne, he established it as his capital. When King Aśoka (無憂王) moved the capital to the city of Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城), he bestowed the city of Rājagṛha upon the Brahmans; therefore, there are no longer any common people in the city, only fewer than a thousand Brahman families. In the southwest corner of the palace city, there are two small monasteries where visiting monks from various countries stay when they come and go; this is the place where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma. To the northwest of this, there is a stūpa, which is the former home of the elder Jyotiṣka (珠底色迦). Outside the south gate of the city, on the left side of the road, there is a stūpa where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and converted Rāhula (羅怙羅).

issues: "The King said that in this original great monastery…" → 帝曰本大伽藍者: 帝曰 is to be read 帝日 = Śakrāditya (= 鑠迦羅阿逸多, the founder): "Śakrāditya's original great monastery now houses a Buddha image…"; no one is speaking (Mizutani: 帝日王の大伽藍; the donor repaid is Śakrāditya); "those who travel here under a false reputation are all treated with courtesy" → 竊名而遊，咸得禮重 "those who travel about falsely claiming its name (as Nālandā students) are everywhere treated with respect" (Mizutani: 虚偽の肩書で諸方に遊ぶとしても); "seventeen or eighteen out of every twenty" → 十七八 "seven or eight in ten"; "the country of China (那國)" → 至那國 Cīna
en_revised: Traveling north from here for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the Nālandā monastery (那爛陀僧伽藍). I heard from the elders that in the mango grove to the south of this monastery there is a pond where a dragon named Nālandā resides; the monastery was built beside it and took its name from the dragon. According to the actual account, when the Tathāgata was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he was a great king who established his capital at this site. He felt compassion for sentient beings and delighted in giving generously; at that time, people praised his virtue and called him "He who is never satiated in giving," and the monastery was named accordingly. The site was originally a mango grove, which five hundred merchants bought for ten billion gold coins and offered to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months, and those merchants all attained the holy fruits. Not long after the Buddha’s nirvana, a former king of this country named Śakrāditya (鑠迦羅阿逸多), who deeply respected the One Vehicle and honored the Triple Gem, selected this auspicious site by divination and built this monastery. When construction first began, the dragon’s body was wounded. At that time, a Nirgrantha outsider skilled in divination saw this and predicted: "This is a superior site; if a monastery is built here, it will surely flourish and become the standard for the five Indias. It will continue to rise for over a thousand years, and later students will easily complete their studies here, yet they will often cough up blood because the dragon was wounded." His son, King Buddhagupta (佛陀毱多), succeeded to the throne and, following the noble legacy, built another monastery to the south of this one. King Tathāgatagupta (呾他揭多毱多) earnestly followed the precedents of his ancestors and built another monastery to the east of this one. When King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多) succeeded to the throne, he built another monastery to the northeast of this one. When the work was completed and the tasks finished, he held a celebratory merit-making assembly, expressing his sincerity to both the hidden and the manifest, and invited both ordinary and holy beings. At this assembly, monks from the five Indias gathered from ten thousand li away. Once the assembly was seated, two monks arrived late and were led up to the third story of the pavilion. Someone asked them, "The King is holding this assembly and has invited both ordinary and holy beings; from what region do you venerable ones come, arriving only at the very end?" They replied, "We have come from the country of Cīna (至那國). Our master was suffering from an illness, so we departed only after he had eaten. Having received the King’s distant invitation, we have come to attend the assembly." The questioner was astonished and immediately reported this to the King. The King realized in his heart that they were holy beings and went in person to inquire of them, but when he arrived at the upper story of the pavilion, he did not know where they had gone. The King’s faith deepened further, and he renounced his kingdom to become a monk. Once he had become a monk, he was ranked at the very end of the assembly, which left him constantly dissatisfied and uneasy, thinking: "I was once a king, occupying the highest and most honorable position; now that I have become a monk, I am in the lowest position among the assembly." He soon went to inform the monks and described his situation. Thereupon, the assembly of monks reached a consensus, decreeing that those who had not yet received the full precepts should be ranked according to their age; this is why this monastery alone has this rule. After the King’s son, Vajra (代闍羅), succeeded to the throne, his faith was firm and steadfast, and he built another monastery to the west of this site. Later, a king of Central India built another great monastery to the north of this location. Thus, the surrounding walls stand high and steep, all enclosed within a single gate. Since successive kings have built them over generations, exhausting all the skills of carving and craftsmanship, it is truly a magnificent sight. In the original great monastery of Śakrāditya (帝日, CBETA 帝曰), a Buddha image is now installed, and forty monks are dispatched from the assembly daily to eat here in order to repay the kindness of the donor. There are several thousand monks, all of whom are brilliant talents and scholars of high learning; those whose virtue is esteemed by their contemporaries and whose reputation has spread to foreign lands number more than several hundred. Their conduct is pure and their observance of the monastic discipline is refined; the monks have strict regulations, and the assembly is entirely upright and simple, such that all the countries of India look to them as a model. They seek instruction and discuss profound mysteries, finding the whole day insufficient; they remain vigilant and admonish one another day and night, with the old and young helping each other to perfection, and if there were any who did not discuss the subtle meanings of the Tripitaka, they would feel ashamed of their own shadows. Therefore, scholars from foreign lands who wish to spread their reputation all come here to resolve their doubts, and only then does their elegant fame flow forth. Thus, even those who travel about falsely claiming its name are everywhere treated with courtesy and respect. When those from distant regions and foreign lands wish to enter for discussion, the gatekeepers pose difficult questions, and many are forced to turn back; only those who are deeply learned in both ancient and modern studies are permitted to enter. Consequently, among the visiting students who discuss their arts and skills in detail, those who are forced to retreat are indeed seven or eight out of every ten. When two or three of the broadly learned ones question them in turn within the assembly, there is none whose sharpness is not blunted and whose reputation is not diminished. As for those of eminent talent and broad learning, possessing strong memories and many abilities, these virtuous and wise men join their brilliance and follow in the footsteps of their predecessors. As for Dharmapāla (護法) and Candrapāla (護月), they stirred the fragrant dust of the Buddha’s legacy; Guṇamati (德慧) and Sthiramati (堅慧) spread their elegant reputations throughout their time; there were the refined discourses of Prabhāmitra (光友) and the lofty conversations of Jinamitra (勝友); Jñānacandra (智月) was clear and keen in his discernment; and Śīlabhadra (戒賢) possessed virtue that was sublime and profound. These superior men were known to all; their virtue excelled that of their predecessors, and their learning encompassed the ancient texts; each composed more than ten treatises and commentaries, which were widely circulated and highly valued by their contemporaries. Around the monastery, there are hundreds of sacred traces; I shall cite two or three of them as a brief summary.

issues: "a fragrant cell (mūla-gandha-kuṭī)" / "the Buddha’s fragrant cell" → the text has 精舍 / 佛精舍 "vihāra", "the Buddha's vihāra" (the Mūlagandhakuṭī identification is Mizutani's, from Yijing)
en_revised: Not far to the west of the monastery (saṃghārāma) is a vihāra (精舍). In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for three months, extensively expounding the wonderful Dharma for the devas and humans. More than one hundred paces to the south is a small stupa, the place where a bhikṣu from a distant land saw the Buddha. Long ago, a bhikṣu came from a distant land and, upon arriving here, encountered the Tathāgata and his holy assembly. Internally giving rise to a heart of reverence, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and immediately made a vow to seek the position of a wheel-turning king (cakravartin). Having seen this, the Tathāgata told the assembly: "That bhikṣu is truly to be pitied. His merit and virtue are deep and far-reaching, and his faith is firm; if he were to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, he would soon attain it. Now, however, he has made a vow to seek the position of a wheel-turning king, and in a future life, he will certainly receive this reward. From the place where his body touched the ground down to the golden wheel, the number of all the minute dust particles contained therein—each and every dust particle represents the reward of a wheel-turning king. Since he indulges in worldly pleasures, the holy fruit is far off." To the south of this is a standing statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Sometimes he is seen holding an incense burner, going toward the Buddha’s vihāra, and circling it to the right. In the stupa to the south of the statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara are the hair and fingernails of the Tathāgata, shorn and clipped during those three months. Those who are afflicted with illness often recover by circumambulating it. The stupa by the side of the pond outside the western wall is where a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), holding a bird, questioned the Buddha about the matter of life and death. More than fifty paces to the southeast, within the enclosure, is a marvelous tree eight or nine feet high with its trunk divided into two; in the past, the Tathāgata chewed a willow twig and threw it on the ground, where it took root, and although a long time has passed, it has neither increased nor decreased. To the east is a great vihara, over two hundred feet high, where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for four months. To the north, one hundred and some paces away, is a vihara containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩). Those of pure faith who come to make offerings see it differently, and its position cannot be fixed; sometimes it stands by the side of the door, and sometimes it appears before the eaves. The clergy and laity of various countries all come to make offerings. To the north of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva vihara is a great vihara, over three hundred feet high, built by King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多王); its ornamentation, dimensions, and the Buddha image within are the same as those of the great vihara under the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree. To its northeast is a stūpa where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for seven days. To the northwest is the place where the four past Buddhas sat. To its south is a brass vihara built by King Śīlāditya (戒日王); although the work is not yet finished, according to its plans and measurements, it will be one hundred feet high when completed. To the east, two hundred and some paces outside the enclosure, is a standing copper Buddha image, over eighty feet high, which required a six-story pavilion to cover it; it was made in the past by King Pūrṇavarman (滿胄王). Two or three li north of the copper Buddha image of King Pūrṇavarman, inside a brick vihara, is an image of the Bodhisattva Tārā (多羅菩薩). Its stature is lofty, and its spiritual efficacy is very manifest. Every year on the first day of the year, grand offerings are made; kings of neighboring regions, ministers, and noble families bring wonderful incense and flowers, hold precious banners and canopies, play metal and stone instruments in succession, and harmonize them with string and bamboo instruments, holding this Dharma assembly for seven days. Inside the south gate of the enclosure, there is a large well. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, a large company of merchants, pressed by heat and thirst, came to where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One pointed to the ground, indicating that water could be obtained there. The leader of the merchants then struck the ground with a cart axle; once the ground was indented, water gushed forth like a spring. Having drunk and heard the Dharma, they all realized the holy fruit.

issues: "King Bimbisāra went to meet the Buddha and traveled more than twenty li to the southeast" → 頻毘娑羅王迎佛東南行二十餘里 is a route statement: "from (the stūpa where) King Bimbisāra met the Buddha, going southeast more than twenty li" (wrong subject)
en_revised: Going more than twenty *li* southeast from the place where King Bimbisāra met the Buddha, one arrives at the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂拏迦邑). In it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the native village of the Venerable Śāriputra, and the well still exists today. Beside it is a stūpa where the Venerable entered into extinction, which contains his bodily relics. The Venerable was of a great Brahmin lineage. His father was highly talented and broadly learned, with a deep insight into the subtle and profound; there was no classic or treatise that he had not thoroughly studied. His wife had a dream and told her husband in detail, saying: "Last night in my sleep, I dreamt of a strange man clad in armor and holding a vajra, who demolished all the mountains and then stood back beneath a single mountain." Her husband said: "This is a very auspicious dream. You will give birth to a son who will be learned and peerless in the world, who will defeat all the masters of debate and shatter their doctrines, but who will be inferior to only one person, to whom he will become a disciple." She was indeed pregnant, and the mother suddenly became intelligent, engaging in high-level discussions and debates with speech that was never obstructed. When the Venerable was eight years old, his fame spread to the four quarters; his nature was pure and simple, his heart was compassionate, he destroyed the bonds of defilement, and he attained wisdom. He and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) were friends from youth and deeply loathed the dusty world, yet they had not found a place to turn. Thereupon, he and Maudgalyāyana went to the place of the non-Buddhist Sañjaya (珊闍耶) to study. They then said to each other: "This is not the ultimate truth, and it cannot exhaust the limits of suffering. Let us each seek a clear guide; whoever tastes the nectar first must share the flavor with the other." At that time, the great arhat Aśvajit (馬勝) held his alms bowl and entered the city to beg for food. Śāriputra (舍利子) saw his dignified and graceful demeanor and immediately asked him, "Who is your teacher?" He replied, "The prince of the Śākya clan, who grew weary of the world, renounced household life, and attained equal and perfect enlightenment—he is my teacher." Śāriputra said, "What dharma does he teach? May I hear it?" He replied, "I have only recently received his instruction and have not yet grasped the profound meaning." Śāriputra said, "I wish to hear what you have learned." Aśvajit then expounded it according to the occasion, and upon hearing it, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit. He then went with his two hundred and fifty disciples to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar, pointed them out, and told the assembly, "Among my disciples, he is the foremost in wisdom." Upon arriving, he prostrated and requested to follow the Buddha's dharma. The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, bhikṣu." Upon hearing these words, his precepts were fully perfected. More than half a month later, he heard the Buddha teaching the dharma to the Long-nailed Ascetic (長爪梵志), and upon hearing the remaining discourse, he was enlightened and attained the fruit of an arhat. Later, when Ānanda (阿難) received the Buddha's announcement of the time of his extinction, the news was passed from one to another, and all were filled with sorrow. Śāriputra’s deep longing and reverence increased, and he could not bear to see the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, so he requested the World-Honored One to let him enter extinction first. The World-Honored One said, "You should know the time." He took leave of his disciples and went to his native village, where his attendant novice informed the entire city. King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) and his subjects, without exception, rushed like the wind and gathered like clouds. Śāriputra spoke extensively on the Dharma, and having heard him, they departed. During the last watch of the night, he focused his mind and entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); upon arising from that meditation, he attained extinction. Four or five li to the southeast of the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂挐迦邑), there is a stūpa at the place where the disciples of the Venerable Śāriputra entered nirvāṇa. Some say that when Kāśyapa Buddha was in the world, three koṭis of great arhats entered nirvāṇa without remainder at this same place.

issues: "the mountain of Vyāsa (孤山)" → 孤山 is "an isolated hill"; no name (the Vyāsa hill is 09.02.03b near Rājagṛha)
en_revised: Two or three li south of the Kapotaka monastery (迦布德迦伽藍), one arrives at an isolated hill (孤山). The mountain is lofty and steep, with lush forests, famous flowers, and clear streams covering the cliffs and lining the ravines. Above, there are many vihāras (精舍) and sacred temples, which are extremely refined in their craftsmanship. In the central vihāra is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); although small in size, its spiritual majesty inspires awe, as it holds a lotus in its hand and bears a Buddha figure upon its crown. There are often people who fast and focus their minds, seeking a vision of the Bodhisattva for seven days, fourteen days, or even a full month; those who receive a response see the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, in all his solemn and wondrous beauty and brilliant radiance, emerge from the statue to comfort and exhort them. Long ago, the king of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) in the South Sea looked into a mirror at dawn and saw not his own reflection, but rather this Bodhisattva statue atop a small hill in the Tāla forest of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in Jambudvīpa (贍部洲); the king, deeply moved and joyful, sought to find it. When he arrived at this hill, he found the statue to be exactly as he had seen, so he built a vihāra and established various offerings. Since then, subsequent kings, admiring this legacy, have built vihāras and sacred temples alongside it, and offerings of incense, flowers, and music have never ceased.

issues: "the isolated hill (Vyāsa 孤山)" → no Vyāsa in the text (cf. 09.03.14)
en_revised: Traveling southeast for more than forty li from the statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) on the isolated hill (孤山), one reaches a monastery where there are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. In front of the monastery is a great stūpa, which possesses many miraculous qualities; it is the place where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma for seven days to the Brahmadeva-rāja and others. Beside it are the sites of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the three past Buddhas.
